reference_choice: pluggable; the shipped default ignores live load entirely and picks at random by declared weight
question: Among the providers that can serve the chosen model, what decides which one gets the request?
default: live remaining headroom and expected time-to-answer together
alternatives: always the first provider that stocks the model
the cheapest provider that stocks the model
the provider with the most remaining headroom
the provider expected to answer soonest
live remaining headroom and expected time-to-answer together
rationale: The reference systems disagree sharply and the shipped fleet makes price, speed and headroom point at three different providers; this is the single largest behavioural choice in the build.

reference_choice: refuse immediately with an explicit rejection; waiting is opt-in per request
question: When no provider can serve a request right now, does the router wait for capacity or refuse the request?
default: wait for capacity, with an explicit give-up point
alternatives: refuse immediately
wait for capacity indefinitely
wait for capacity, with an explicit give-up point
rationale: Refusing is scored as a violated SLO AND zero quality here, so instant refusal is expensive; but waiting indefinitely is a typed loss. The give-up point is the real question.

reference_choice: prefer a different target with zero delay; back off only when no alternative exists
question: After an attempt is rejected, should the next attempt go to a different provider or wait and retry the same one?
default: a different provider first, waiting only when no alternative exists
alternatives: wait and retry the same provider
a different provider first, waiting only when no alternative exists
give up after a fixed number of attempts
rationale: Both production gateways prefer diverting over waiting, and the shipped fleet always has at least one other provider stocking the same model.

reference_choice: retries are never gated on idempotency; even an authentication failure is retried when the group has more than one target
question: May any request be retried, or only the ones declared safe to repeat?
default: only requests declared safe to repeat
alternatives: any request may be retried
only requests declared safe to repeat
rationale: The shipped Request carries an explicit retry_safe flag, and the most-cited reference system ignores the equivalent distinction, which is exactly the production bug class this run should avoid.

reference_choice: a fixed short quarantine, then re-probe with real traffic
question: Once a provider is known to be unavailable, when may the router send it real traffic again?
default: not before the announced end of its unavailability
alternatives: immediately, on every request
after a fixed waiting period
not before the announced end of its unavailability
rationale: The shipped fleet publishes an explicit end-of-outage time, so re-probing early is pure loss; dispatching into an announced outage past a grace of 8 attempts loses the request outright.

reference_choice: reserve request slots before the call, charge tokens after
question: How should the router stay inside a provider's published request and token allowance?
default: subtract the request's own expected consumption from the published headroom before dispatching
alternatives: dispatch and learn from rejections
subtract the request's own expected consumption from the published headroom before dispatching
keep a reserve of headroom unused so a burst has somewhere to land
rationale: The fleet publishes live remaining request and token headroom and the request declares its own expected token consumption, so pre-emptive pacing is available here in a way it is not in the reference systems; the reserve variant is what the shipped baseline does.

reference_choice: hard caps per provider and per tag that filter candidates before placement
question: Is spend bounded by anything other than the traffic itself?
default: a price-aware preference with no hard ceiling
alternatives: no cost consideration at all
a price-aware preference with no hard ceiling
a hard spend ceiling per window that changes behaviour once crossed
rationale: Production gateways ship hard caps; the offline routing literature ships only soft preferences. Cost carries weight 3.0 in the scored objective.

reference_choice: per-caller consumption quotas, with nothing reserved
question: On a shared fleet, what stops one traffic shape from starving another?
default: each traffic shape is capped at what it may consume
alternatives: nothing: first come, first served
each traffic shape is capped at what it may consume
each traffic shape is guaranteed a reserved share of capacity
rationale: The two tenants here share one saturating provider and are scored separately, so whether the specialist may take capacity from the other tenant is a real and consequential choice.

reference_choice: the full attempt chain and its cost travel back with the answer
question: What must an operator be able to see after a request goes wrong?
default: which provider served it, how many attempts it took, and why each earlier attempt failed
alternatives: nothing
which provider served it
which provider served it, how many attempts it took, and why each earlier attempt failed
rationale: Both production gateways surface the attempt chain; nothing the router reports can move the score, so this is pure operator value at no risk.
